course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Cold War and Decolonization
unit.description: Study how the Cold War divided the world, how colonies won independence, how new states and movements challenged established power, and why the Cold War ended.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.7 key concept: movements used nonviolent resistance to challenge discrimination and colonial or minority rule
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the US civil rights movement and the struggle against apartheid, 1948–1994
stimulusBlocks.text:
In the United States, Martin Luther King Jr. drew on Gandhi's example. The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956 and the March on Washington in 1963 helped win the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In South Africa, the white minority government imposed apartheid after 1948. The African National Congress at first used nonviolent protest, but after police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960 and the government banned the party, it formed an armed wing. Nelson Mandela spent twenty-seven years in prison before he was released in 1990. In 1994 he was elected president in South Africa's first election open to all races.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a difference between the movements in the passage?
choices: Only the US movement opposed segregation

Only the ANC drew on Gandhi's example
Only the US movement succeeded
questions.explanation: The ANC turned to armed struggle after being banned.
choiceExplanations: Both opposed segregation.
The ANC turned to armed struggle after being banned.
The passage links King, not the ANC, to Gandhi.
Apartheid ended in 1994.
questions.distinguisher: The passage names Gandhi as King's influence, not the ANC's.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.7 key concept: some groups challenged existing power through violence, and some governments responded to protest with force
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing armed movements and state repression, 1968–1992
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1968, reformers in Czechoslovakia tried to create “socialism with a human face,” loosening censorship. In August, Warsaw Pact armies invaded and ended the Prague Spring.

In Peru, the Maoist Shining Path began an armed campaign in 1980 to overthrow the government. Its attacks on villages, and the army's brutal response, left tens of thousands dead before its leader was captured in 1992.

questions.explanation: Invasion in Czechoslovakia and army brutality in Peru show violent responses.
choiceExplanations: The Shining Path used violence.
Invasion in Czechoslovakia and army brutality in Peru show violent responses.
The Warsaw Pact crushed the reforms.
The Shining Path failed.
questions.distinguisher: The Prague reformers were peaceful, but the Shining Path was not.

questions.prompt: Why was the salt tax an effective target for Gandhi's campaign?
choices: It was the largest source of revenue for the British Empire
It was collected only from the wealthy Indian princes
It hit poor Indians and symbolized British control
It was a new tax introduced by Britain in 1930
questions.explanation: The passage says the tax fell heavily on the poor, and the salt monopoly showed British power over everyday life.
choiceExplanations: The passage does not claim the tax was the largest source of revenue.
The passage says the burden fell on poor Indians.
The passage says the tax fell heavily on the poor, and the salt monopoly showed British power over everyday life.
The salt monopoly and tax were long-standing, not new in 1930.
questions.distinguisher: The tax raised revenue, but its value for the campaign lay in its meaning for ordinary people.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.7 key concept: movements used nonviolent resistance to challenge colonial rule
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Gandhi's Salt March, 1930
stimulusBlocks.text:
In March 1930, Mohandas Gandhi led a march of several dozen followers from his ashram near Ahmedabad to the Arabian Sea coast at Dandi, about 240 miles away, where he picked up natural salt. British law gave the government a monopoly on salt and taxed it, a burden that fell heavily on poor Indians.

Thousands of Indians soon made or sold salt in defiance of the law, and about 60,000 people were arrested, including Gandhi. The campaign drew worldwide press attention. Gandhi called his method satyagraha, a commitment to truth through nonviolent noncooperation. The campaign did not end British rule, but it showed that the Indian National Congress could mobilize millions of people across class and region.

The 1857 rebellion was an armed revolt that came before Gandhi.
The Algerian struggle was an armed war.
The Maji Maji Rebellion was an armed uprising that preceded the Salt March.
questions.distinguisher: The 1857 rebellion also challenged British rule, but it came earlier and used armed force.
